Neonates of the White-beaked dolphin enter the world at an average body length of 120 centimeters [Lb = 120 centimeters], a measurement that aligns with the species' moderately large body size at parturition compared to other delphinids. At a core body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C], the newborn calves typically weigh approximately 40,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 40,000 grams], reflecting a substantial investment of maternal resources into a single, well-developed offspring. This considerable birth mass is thought to confer advantages in thermoregulation in the cold North Atlantic waters the species inhabits, as a larger body surface-to-volume ratio reduces heat loss. The calves are precocial, capable of swimming and surfacing to breathe within moments of the birth event, and they rely entirely on their mother's milk during the initial phase of life. The onset of lactation is immediate, and the suckling juvenile begins a period of rapid growth that is sustained by the rich, high-fat milk characteristic of cetaceans.

Remarkable sexual dimorphism in body size becomes apparent as individuals approach adulthood, with males ultimately reaching a greater asymptotic length. At a core body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C], adult females typically attain a maximum total length of 250 centimeters [Li = 250 centimeters], while adult males can reach up to 267 centimeters [Li = up to 267 centimeters], a difference of roughly seven percent that is consistent with patterns observed in other Lagenorhynchus species. This size disparity is also reflected in the ultimate wet weights: females achieve an adult body mass of roughly 306,000 grams [Wwi = roughly 306,000 grams], whereas males can attain up to 354,000 grams [Wwi = up to 354,000 grams]. Such sexual size dimorphism is often linked to intrasexual competition among males for access to receptive females, a behavior documented in several related dolphin species. These estimates of adult body mass derive from a combination of stranding records and bycatch data collected across the species' range in the North Atlantic, providing a robust baseline for understanding the energetic demands of this apex predator.

The timing of sexual maturation in White-beaked dolphins shows clear sex-specific differences, a pattern commonly reported in odontocetes. At a core body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C], females reach puberty at a total length of approximately 234 centimeters [Lp = approximately 234 centimeters], corresponding to a period of roughly 7 years after birth [tp = roughly 7 years after birth]. Males, in contrast, achieve sexual maturity at a slightly greater length, approximately 244 centimeters [Lp = approximately 244 centimeters], and require about 8 years after birth [tp = about 8 years after birth] to reach this developmental milestone at a temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]. The later maturation of males is consistent with their larger ultimate body size and the need for a prolonged growth phase before reproductive investment can begin. These values are based on analyses of gonadal development in specimens collected from fisheries interactions in the Northeast Atlantic, and they provide critical data for population viability models.

Reproductive output in this species is comparatively low, consistent with a slow life-history strategy typical of large-bodied cetaceans. The estimated maximum reproductive output, based on a core body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C], involves females producing one calf per calving event [N_R_i = one calf per calving event] with an annual frequency of one calving event per year [F_R_i = one calving event per year]. Following birth, the calf is nursed for an extended period before achieving nutritional independence; the time since birth at weaning is suspected to be approximately 365 days since birth [tx = approximately 365 days since birth], a figure extrapolated from observations of the closely related common dolphin (Delphinus delphis) and plausible given the species' life history at a temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]. The gestation time in White-beaked dolphins is not directly known, but based on data from the dusky dolphin (Lagenorhynchus obscurus) it is estimated to be around 393 days [tg = around 393 days] at a temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]. This protracted gestation period is followed by an equally long period of lactation, ensuring the calf is well-developed before facing the challenges of independent foraging.

Longevity in White-beaked dolphins is considerable, with the maximum lifespan estimated at approximately 14,600 days [am = approximately 14,600 days], a figure derived from long-term photo-identification studies and analyses of growth layer groups in tooth sections, standardized to a core body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to about 40 years, is typical for a delphinid of its size and places the species within the range of other long-lived marine mammals. Such an extended period of somatic maintenance and reproductive activity allows for multiple breeding events over an individual's lifetime, a pattern that is common among species with low annual fecundity. The species is known to form mixed-sex groups that can number in the dozens, and foraging behavior often involves cooperative hunting of schooling fish such as herring and gadids. These social and ecological traits, combined with the species' relatively high adult survival rates, suggest a stable life-history strategy adapted to the productive but seasonally variable waters of the North Atlantic and adjacent seas.
